newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria c/a deficit eases as EU transfers fall.
newsitem.headline: Austria c/a deficit eases as EU transfers fall.

text.p: Austria's 1996 current account deficit eased to 42.4 million schillings from 47 million a year earlier, the first decline since 1990, the Austrian National Bank said on Friday.
It traced the improvement in the country's external balance to lower net transfers to the European Union (EU), which Austria joined in 1995.
Austria paid 26 billion schillings into the EU's coffers, but received some 23 billion schillings from the EU in subsidies and other payments.
But the central bank warned that the deficit, at 1.8 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), was still at an alarmingly high level.
"This is a level that still gives rise to very serious concerns," executive director Thomas Lachs told a news conference.

He said there was little hope that the deficit could be reduced significantly in 1997. "We expect only a slight reduction of the deficit," Lachs said, adding that only a level of around one percent of GDP was sustainable in the long term.
"Higher exports are the only way we can get our current acount under control," he said. "Strong efforts will be necessary to succeed in balancing the account."
The central bank said that the slump in Austria' tourism earnings, caused by the strong schilling and the lure of cheap destinations elsewhere, was unlikely to end soon.
"Even under the most optimistic assumptions we will not be able to show the same surplus we had three years ago," he said.

Tourism income fell to 23.1 billion schillings, from 29.7 billion a year earlier, as the number of overnight stays in Austria dropped 3.2 percent to 84 million. At the same time, Austrians spent seven percent more money abroad then they did in 1995.

According to the bank's data, exports of goods and services rose to 771.5 billion schillings from 732.8 billion a year earlier, while imports rose to 848.0 billion from 805.7 billion, causing a trade deficit of 76.6 billion schillings. -- Vienna newsroom +431 53112 274
